cultivar: Fenghuang Shui Xian, Ye Lai Xiang strain
processing: Sun-withered, shaken overnight to a medium-light oxidation, fixed, rolled into long strips and charcoal roasted light to medium; makers keep the roast restrained to protect its heady night-flower aroma.
harvest_season: Spring, roughly late April into May, with timing depending on the garden and its elevation; the tea is usually picked once.
appearance_dry: Long, tightly twisted olive-brown strips with a heady, sweet floral smell.
appearance_wet: Long, thick yellow-green leaves with red edges.
taste_profile: An intense, almost heady white-flower aroma like tuberose or night-blooming jasmine, a medium body with honey and a juicy sweetness, and a long, cooling finish with a light grip.

brewing.notes: Boiling water, thin gaiwan, flash steeps. The aroma is powerful enough to drink from larger cups than usual; keep pours instant for the first four steeps or the sweetness turns sharp.

vintage_note: Sold by harvest year, usually from late summer or autumn after a light-to-medium roast and a rest; best within one to two years for the aroma, with medium-roasted lots keeping three years sealed and dry. Production is small and the name is mostly found with Chaozhou specialists.
description:
Ye Lai Xiang, fragrance that comes at night, is named for the tuberose, the white flower that releases its scent after dark, and the dancong that carries the name is one of the headiest in the family: a long-leaf Phoenix oolong whose aroma fills the room when the lid comes off. It is one of the ten classic aroma types and one of the less common.

The name covers an aroma type rather than one tree: selections from the Fenghuang Shui Xian population above Chaozhou, propagated by cuttings, with local names such as Beitou Ye Lai Xiang telling them apart. There is not a great deal of it and it rarely reaches the supermarket end of the dancong market.

It is made in the standard way, sun-withered, shaken through the night to a medium-light oxidation, rolled into strips and charcoal roasted, with the roast kept light to medium. The aroma is the point: tuberose, night-blooming jasmine, a sweetness close to honey, and under it a medium body with a juicy quality and a long, cool finish with a light grip.

Brew it with the full Chaozhou method, a thin gaiwan well filled, boiling water, instant pours for the early steeps, and consider slightly larger cups, since the aroma has enough power to carry. It runs eight infusions and is best in the first five. It is a tea for the evening, which is also when its namesake flower performs.

It is sold by year, mostly through Chaozhou specialists, and should be drunk within a year or two for the aroma. The name is sometimes applied loosely to any strongly floral dancong, so buy from sellers who state the strain, village and harvest. If you like heady florals, Ya Shi Xiang is the obvious comparison, brighter and more honeysuckle; Ye Lai Xiang is deeper and more night-time.
history:
Ye Lai Xiang is one of the ten aroma types of Phoenix dancong, named because the cup recalls the night-scented flower. The name marks an aroma family more than one plant: local naming adds a place when it must tell trees apart, as in Beitou Ye Lai Xiang.

Little is documented about its origin, its first trees or when the name came into use, so any precise story about it deserves caution.
